That being said, it is also important to put virtual currency in perspective as a payment

This relative volume of transactions becomes important when you consider that,
according to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, the best estimate for the amount of
all global criminal proceeds available for laundering through the financial system in 2009 was

statutory.question: Does the conduct described fall within 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) — Suspicious activity reporting requirements?
statutory.answer: Neutral — 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) suspicious activity reporting requirements may be implicated, but the facts do not establish that a covered “financial institution” detected the activity or had a SAR-filing obligation triggered under implementing regulations.
statutory.label: neutral
statutory.reasoning: 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) authorizes/mandates suspicious activity reporting by a covered “financial institution” when it detects a possible violation of law or suspicious transaction, as implemented by Treasury/FinCEN regulations (e.g., SAR rules). Element-by-element: (1) Covered reporter: § 5318(g) applies to “financial institutions” (as defined in the BSA framework). The fact pattern describes Entity SYN_e7644811 as a convenience/grocery store (a business customer), not a bank/MSB/broker-dealer/etc., and does not identify any specific financial institution involved in processing the wire or responsible for SAR filing. Without a specified covered financial institution, applicability cannot be determined. (2) Detection of suspicious transaction: The single wire of $229,004.66 to a Hong Kong counterparty with notes “trade-finance over-invoiced,” and the amount far exceeding the declared expected monthly volume, are indicia that could be suspicious, but § 5318(g) requires the reporting obligation to attach to the financial institution upon detection under applicable thresholds and rules; the record does not state who detected it, whether it was flagged, or whether regulatory thresholds/criteria were met. Therefore, § 5318(g) suspicious activity reporting requirements cannot be conclusively applied or excluded on these facts.
